metaData.originalTitle: 图灵奖得主，要用十亿美金赌 AI 的下一个十年（上集）
metaData.title: Turing Award Winner Bets $1 Billion on AI's Next Decade (Part 1)
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article outlines Turing Award winner Yann LeCun's systematic critique of the mainstream large language model approach and details his non-generative alternative, centered on JEPA and world models, backed by a roughly $1 billion bet.
metaData.summary: Based on Yann LeCun's interview on the popular science channel Welch Labs, the article systematically presents his core views on the current trajectory of AI development. It begins with LeCun's academic starting point—convolutional neural networks (CNNs)—leading to his concerns about supervised learning's reliance on labeled data, and revisits his famous "cake theory" (where self-supervised learning is the main body). The article then explains why self-supervised generative methods succeed with language (GPT series) but encounter the "curse of fuzziness" in video—because the prediction space for video is continuous and infinite, forcing models to output averages. LeCun thus poses a key question: must models be generative? He introduces the non-generative "joint embedding" approach (e.g., Siamese networks) and details the challenge of "representation collapse," along with how methods like Barlow Twins (redundancy reduction), VICReg, and the DINO series gradually solve it, eventually matching supervised learning in image classification. The core of the article introduces LeCun's ultimate solution: the world model, specifically implemented as JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture). JEPA's key idea is to make predictions in an abstract embedding space rather than at the pixel level, thereby bypassing the "curse of fuzziness." The article concludes that LeCun believes a true intelligent agent must be able to anticipate the consequences of its own actions, and that the autoregressive prediction of LLMs cannot achieve this, hence his bet on world models as the path to autonomous machine intelligence.

mainPoints.point: LeCun believes the generative approach of large language models (LLMs) cannot lead to true intelligence.
mainPoints.explanation: The core argument is the "curse of fuzziness": in continuous, high-dimensional spaces like video, generative models cannot handle infinite possibilities, can only predict fuzzy averages, and fail to learn a true understanding of the world.

mainPoints.point: The non-generative "joint embedding" method is a superior path for self-supervised learning.
mainPoints.explanation: By forcing the model to generate similar embedding vectors for different views of the same scene (e.g., original and corrupted versions) rather than generating pixels, the "curse of fuzziness" can be avoided, and more robust representations can be learned.

mainPoints.point: "Representation collapse" is the main challenge for joint embedding methods, and solutions like Barlow Twins provide an effective remedy.
mainPoints.explanation: The model might cheat by outputting the same vector for all inputs. Barlow Twins forces the model to learn discriminative features by decorrelating the outputs of different neurons (making the cross-correlation matrix approach the identity matrix), thus avoiding collapse.

mainPoints.point: LeCun's ultimate solution is the "world model," with JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture) as its core architecture.
mainPoints.explanation: JEPA makes predictions in an abstract embedding space, not at the pixel level. It combines a joint embedding architecture with a predictor, allowing it to predict the representation of the world's next state conditioned on actions or control signals, which can then be used for planning and control.

mainPoints.point: LeCun is betting roughly $1 billion, believing that a true intelligent agent must be able to anticipate the consequences of its own actions.
mainPoints.explanation: He argues that the autoregressive reasoning of LLMs is inadequate for this task, and that "search"-based reasoning using world models is key to achieving reliable and safe autonomous machine intelligence.

keyQuotes: The large language models we are all-in on simply cannot lead to true intelligence.
If intelligence is a cake, the bulk of the cake is self-supervised learning, the icing is supervised learning, and the cherry on top is reinforcement learning.
I cannot understand how you can build an intelligent agent on top of a system that cannot predict the consequences of its own actions.
A truly reliable intelligent agent must be able to anticipate the results of a sequence of actions, then plan a path and maintain safety boundaries.

relatedArticles.title: Envisioning the Possible Future of Multimodal Understanding: From Describing the World to Entering the World
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores the future evolution of multimodal understanding, arguing that it should progress from static, offline, question-answering capabilities to dynamic, online world-understanding systems with long-term memory and decision-making participation, and elaborates on six key trends: native multimodality, streaming video understanding, long-term memory, multimodal retrieval, serving as a judge for generative models, and spatial intelligence.

relatedArticles.title: 1.2k Stars in a Week, a Dark Horse Emerges in a Hot Track! Interview with Multica's Zhang Jiayuan: How to Rewrite the Rules of 'Human-AI Collaboration'?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article is an in-depth interview with Zhang Jiayuan, founder of the AI collaboration platform Multica, exploring how its kanban-style interface enables efficient 'multi-human + multi-agent' collaboration, and sharing the team's real-world experience using agents and their thoughts on AI-native organizational structures.

relatedArticles.title: Turing Award Winner LeCun on the Next Step for Large Models
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically reviews Turing Award winner Yann LeCun's judgment on the future direction of large models: LLMs are not the endpoint of general intelligence, with their core gaps being the lack of ability to predict action consequences and perform multi-step planning based on search, and provides a detailed interpretation of LeCun's proposed World Model and JEPA architecture as an alternative path.

relatedArticles.title: 2026: The End of Software, the Fall of Engineers, the Disappearance of Mediocrity
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Using the sharp decline in US software stocks in early 2026 as a starting point, this article deeply analyzes how AI Agents are eroding the SaaS middle-layer business model, and explores structural shifts in software form from product to medium, and the engineer's role from writing code to understanding systems.

relatedArticles.title: “Is AGI Here? I Used It for a Week and My Scalp Tingled” | A Conversation with Zhang Haoran: Co-founder of Moxt
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through an in-depth interview with Moxt co-founder Zhang Haoran, this article explores how AI Native Workspaces are reshaping file systems and collaboration models to evolve organizations from 'human-computer interaction' to 'AI team collaboration.'

relatedArticles.title: The Super Individual | To The Crazy Ones
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the essence of the 'Super Individual,' arguing it is not a result of skill training but a fundamental personality structure driven by curiosity, and suggests that large companies should inspire rather than cultivate such individuals by providing complete closed loops.

relatedArticles.title: What Are We Really Discussing When We Talk About Harness? | In-Depth Dialogue: MiniMax × Hermes Agent
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article compiles an in-depth dialogue hosted by Crossroads, featuring the MiniMax Agent team and the head of Hermes Agent. It delves into the core topics surrounding the shift in hype from OpenClaw to Hermes, exploring the definitions of Agent and Harness, multi-agent collaboration, self-evolution, the gap between Chinese and US models, and entrepreneurial opportunities in Agent Infra.
